title: Chapter 33 – The Spring Register
html:
[Lin Clan – Lin Jian]

On the morning he turns ten, Lin Jian wakes before the cock and counts what he has.

```
[ARK-7 :: Status — Lin Jian]
Qi Refining: Stage 6 (late)
Body: Skin Tempering complete; Flesh Tempering — early stage
Spiritual sense: ~400 paces (ordinary), 40 paces (deep scan)
Interface: Level 2
CE: 171 / 400
Level 3: requires CE 200 and Qi Refining Stage 8
```

Twenty-nine short. Two stages short. He lies in the dark with his hands folded on his chest and lets the numbers settle. The right arm no longer aches. The meridian burn from the night of the ring has healed to a thin silver line he can feel only when he runs the Five-Gate Wheel, a small cold catch at the elbow where the water gate passes into wood. It costs him about four percent of every circuit. He has stopped resenting it.

Lin Yue's voice floats in from the next room, muffled by a quilt. "It is your birthday. You are not allowed to be awake yet."

"I am not awake."

"You are breathing like a person who is awake."

He gives up and sits. Through the paper window the sky is the gray of old pewter, and the pines on the east ridge are thin dark lines. It is the last week of spring. The first warm air of the year has crept into the house, and under it, faint and sour, he can smell the smoke from Hu's granary, where the old man has been up since midnight feeding the fire.

Today is not for the forge. Today the family goes to Willow Ford, to the Registry Hall, to write a name in a book.

* * *

There are five of them on the road. Father rides the gray mule with his left hand loose on the rein, and the Patriarch's pine-crest cloak, one size too large, folds over the mule's flank like a spare blanket. Feng walks at his stirrup in a new gray tunic with his spear on his back, taller than the mule's ears now, broad in the shoulders and sixteen years old. Mother walks a few paces behind, a gardener's hat on her head, as unremarkable as a woman can be who is carrying a knife across the small of her back. Fourth Uncle Wenshi and four guards bring up the rear.

And Jian, who rides in the cart with the baggage, because he is ten and the Patriarch's younger son and nobody expects him to do anything else.

The cart contains the clan register in a lacquered case, a tin of seals, three sets of formal robes, and a basket of dried plums for the registrar's wife. It also contains, in a place the guards have not noticed, a stack of Mirror Guard talismans for the market warden, wrapped in oiled paper. Father drew them last night, forty in a sitting, and did not once look at the clock.

The road to Willow Ford runs down the valley for six hours, through the pine belt and out onto the river plain. Jian counts the milestones. He counts the herds on the near bank, the number of men working the rice paddies, the number of those men who stop to watch the Lin cart go by. At the second ford a boy on a water buffalo raises a hand. At the fourth, a woman in a gray veil looks long at the pine crest on his father's cloak and turns to speak to a man beside her.

Eleven watchers by the third hour. Two of them are looking at the guards. Nine are looking at Father.

He takes a dried plum from the basket and does not eat it.

On the plain the air grows warm and loud. Willow Ford rises out of the haze in brown roofs and blue-tiled gables, a town of perhaps four thousand people on a bend of the river, with the Sect's three-cloud banner above the market gate and the stone wall of the Registry Hall just visible behind it. The streets are packed. Hawkers shout. A man selling Fire Starter slips by the dozen holds them up like fans, and a boy with a tray of Light Orb charms trots alongside the cart until a guard waves him away.

Jian watches the Fire Starter man. The slips are cheap, thin, coarse-grained paper with ink that has bled at the edges. He estimates the circuit efficiency at fifty percent at best. The man is selling them at half a copper each and still not selling them quickly.

The Pavilion undersells everyone, he thinks. And the paper the Lin shop makes is better than anything on this street. That has to count for something.

It has to count for more than it does. A month ago, Wenjun showed him the shop's accounts, because he had asked, and because she thought it was funny that a boy would want to see them. The shop sells forty percent of what it sold two years ago. Customers like the Lin talismans. They simply cannot afford to buy as many.

* * *

The Registry Hall is a low gray building, long and plain, with a roof of black tile and a single door of oiled cedar. It sits at the end of a paved yard and has the look of a place where nobody has ever laughed. Above the lintel hangs the three-cloud crest of the Azure Cloud Sect, carved in stone and weathered nearly smooth.

The yard is full. Twelve tributary houses are registering this season, and each has brought its own retinue. Jian counts seven different crests as the cart rolls through the gate. A thin man in a river-green robe stares at the Lin pine crest as though it has insulted him. A girl of thirteen in a flame-colored cloak leans against a pillar, bored, with a short sword in her belt. Two guards in black mantle armor stand at the Hall door, and they are Sect disciples, not mortal militia. He feels the weight of their Qi on his skin from forty paces, steady and bright, like a lamp that has never been turned down.

Stage 8 or 9, both. They are standing perfectly still. It is a courtesy to the Sect, not a rule.

He sets his breathing into the Still Water Veil and lets the world go dim.

It is a small, practiced motion now, as natural as lowering his eyes. Mother taught it to him on a winter morning four years ago, in the cold kitchen, with a bowl of water between them and her palm over his. A lake in winter, she had said. Not frozen. Just quiet. He draws his Qi inward until the surface of it goes flat. The edges of it fold under. A person standing beside him now would feel a boy of nine, perhaps ten, with a first-layer glimmer of Qi, the kind of child you find in any farming house in the valley.

He keeps it there. It costs him nothing to maintain, and everything to forget.

The registrar is a gaunt man named Gao, with a long nose, ink on his cuffs and a brush stuck behind his ear. He comes to the yard to receive them in person, which, Jian understands from the faint stiffening in Wenshi's shoulders, is an unusual honor.

"Patriarch Lin." He bows exactly as deep as the Compact requires. "The Arbiter will see you at the third bell. In the meantime I must ask the family to register its minors. It is a formality. We register all minors in the house when the head changes, in case of disputes."

"Of course," Father says.

"Lin Yue, six, root: none." Gao writes it without looking up. "Lin Jian, ten, root: pseudo-root, five crystals." He glances at Jian, and then at a small gray jade the size of a plum that sits on the desk. "I am required to test the cultivation level of minors by the Sect's own measure. It will take a moment. Hold the jade in your right hand."

Jian takes it. It is warm and faintly humming, and he feels, through the skin of his palm, a thread of Qi tasting its way up his arm. Not forcing. Asking. The way a clerk asks a question: politely, with an answer already half decided.

It is a mortal-grade sensing jade. Weak. It reads exactly what the Veil lets it read.

He lets it read the Veil.

The jade glows a dim, steady green. Gao nods and writes. "Qi Refining, second stage. Spiritual sense unremarkable." He looks up. "Your grandfather said you were a late bloomer."

"I am slow, sir," Jian says.

"There is no shame in that." Gao's face does not change, but his voice goes briefly human. "My own son took five years to pass the second stage. He is a very good accountant now."

Behind them, in the doorway, someone laughs.

It is a short, soft sound, and he knows it before he turns. He turns anyway, slowly, the way a boy of ten would turn, with a plum in one hand and a jade in the other.

Zhao Qian stands in the Hall doorway, under the carved crest.

He is twenty now. Tall, straight-backed and spare, in a green robe with the Red Ridge crest on the breast. He wears a silver-gray cloak thrown back from his shoulders, and his right arm lies bound against his chest in a splint of black iron and leather. The wrist beneath the splint is the wrong shape. It healed, but it healed badly, and the hand at the end of it hangs like a glove. He holds his saber in the left hand, the point of the sheath down, and he holds it badly.

He is smiling. It is not a pleasant smile, and it has been practiced.

"Patriarch Lin." The bow is flawless. "I did not know the Lin house was registering today. How fortunate. I am here on Red Ridge's business, and I would not have wanted to miss it."

"Young Master Zhao," Father says. He does not smile. "I trust your uncle is recovering."

"My uncle thanks you for your concern." Qian's voice is smooth. "He is well enough to have letters read to him. He asked me to send his condolence on your father's death. He wished it noted that Lin Zhenshan was the finest swordsman he has ever fought." A very small pause. "He said it was a pity that such a man should die for a stone hut."

Do not answer. Jian does not move. Do not answer. Do not look at him. He wants a reaction.

"My father would have liked to hear it," Father says, without any expression at all.

"I am certain." Qian's gaze moves along the Lin party, like a man counting coins. Wenshi's hand rests on the hilt at his belt. Mother stands at the back with her hat in her hand. Feng is looking straight ahead at a spot on the wall with an expression that would crack stone. "Triple root," Qian murmurs. "Sixteen. The Outer Court will be glad."

"They will," Feng says, in a very quiet voice.

"I hope you do well there. I mean it." And then, in the same light tone: "You have a younger brother, I think. The one with the five crystals."

His eyes find Jian, and for a moment the entire yard narrows to the space between them.

Qian does not scan him. It would be a breach, and he knows it, and in any case his spiritual sense has been bent since the day of the ring. He only looks. He looks the way a man looks at a locked door he has been told is empty.

"A quiet boy," he says. "My uncle was curious about him. He is curious about everything on this hill. It is a failing of the old." He smiles again. "Do you read, Lin Jian?"

"A little, sir," Jian says.

"A little." Qian lets the words sit. "My uncle says that the best readers can see what is written on the inside of a closed book. I have never believed him. But he is a patient man, and he reads a great deal."

Then he turns and goes into the Hall, the saber swinging awkwardly at his left hip, and the door closes behind him with a soft sound.

Nobody speaks. Wenshi lets out his breath through his nose.

"That," Mother says quietly, from the back, "was a courtesy visit."

Jian looks at the closed door. His hand has closed so tightly around the plum that the skin has split and the juice has run down his wrist. He opens his fingers and looks at the mess, and then, carefully, wipes it on his sleeve.

Inside of a closed book.

He knows. No. He suspects. He has no proof, and he has been told there is nothing to find, and he is afraid of it anyway. He feels something cold and very clear move through his thoughts. Qian is the sort who would break my arm in a dark corridor if no one were looking. He is also the sort who would have to be sure first.

I am not going to give him a reason to be sure.

* * *

The Arbiter sees them at the third bell, in a high bare room with a floor of black stone and a table of plain pine.

Shen Wuye sits behind the table in a gray robe, with a brush in his hand and a stack of papers at his elbow. Jian remembers him from the hearing at the spring: a lean man with a square gray beard and eyes that rest on a person a moment longer than comfort allows. He rises as they enter, and bows to Father, a bare half inch less than the bow to a Patriarch but a full inch more than the bow to a stranger.

"Patriarch Lin," he says. "I am sorry about your father."

"Thank you, Arbiter."

"I knew him a little. Not well enough to say anything useful." Shen lowers himself back into his chair. "Sit. The register is ready. We have much to settle and not very long to settle it in."

Father sits. Feng, at a nod, stands behind him. Jian is put on a bench at the wall with Yue, who has fallen asleep against his shoulder, and he is grateful for it. A child asleep is a child nobody looks at.

Shen reads the formal entry aloud. His voice is dry and precise. The house of Lin of Green Pine Hill, tributary to the Azure Cloud Sect by the Vassal Compact, holder of the land called Green Pine by deed, registered the founder's seal. The late Patriarch, Lin Zhenshan, deceased in the sixth month of the previous year. The surviving son, Lin Wenyuan, entering the chair by right of the eldest and by acclamation of the council.

"It is in order," Shen says. "I will enter it." He dips his brush. "And the heir?"

"My son Lin Feng," Father says. His voice does not shake. "Sixteen years old. Triple root, wood, fire and earth. Qi Refining, stage seven."

"I would like to see it."

Feng steps forward. Shen produces a small bronze mirror, the size of a hand, and lays it on the table between them. Feng puts his palm on it. For a breath the mirror clouds. Then three colors rise from the center and stand upright in the air, green, red and brown, each as tall as a finger, burning with a clean steady light. The red is brightest. The green is nearly as bright.

Somewhere in the Hall, a bell rings, once, very low.

"Triple root," Shen says. "Qi Refining seven. I confirm." He writes. The brush makes a dry, careful sound. "Lin Feng, son of Lin Wenyuan, heir to the house of Green Pine. Registered at the Spring Register, in the presence of the Arbiter." He lifts the brush. "It is done. The Headless House clause lapses as of this hour."

Father closes his eyes for just a moment.

"There is a petition on file," Shen continues in the same level voice, "which you inquired about in your letter. I will tell you what I can. It is the petition submitted by Lin Wenhai last winter under the clause, in his own hand, with his name and seal. It was not amended. It has not been withdrawn, because a dead man cannot withdraw. It remains on file until an heir is registered." He turns the page. "An heir has been registered. The petition is void. I have written it so."

"Last winter," Father repeats. "Before he fled."

"Before he fled. Yes." Shen looks at him. "Your inference in the letter was that someone had signed it afterward. I considered it. I looked at the ink and the sealing wax. The date is correct. The signature is his."

"Then there is no new petition."

"There is no new petition from the Lins." Shen lays down the brush. "I will add, since I think you should know it, that the Hall received a second communication in the same week from Red Ridge. It asked, in general terms, whether the house of Lin was in a condition to defend its own boundaries. It asked whether the arbiter's report on the midsummer incident had been shared with the Sect's inspectors. It asked whether a Patriarch might be required to submit to a Hall audit after a period of disorder." He pauses. "I answered all three. The answers were yes, yes, and yes."

The room is very quiet.

"An audit," Wenyuan says.

"A routine one. It follows any change of Patriarch in a tributary house, and the Hall has been slow to schedule it because the late Patriarch's death was complicated." Shen's face does not change. "An inspector will be assigned. I cannot tell you when. It will not be me. I have too many entanglements with your hill." A slight dry inflection. "He will examine the tribute rolls, the deed, the treasury and the guard. He is a man named Cheng Yun, in the middle stage of Foundation Establishment. He has the reputation of being honest. I would advise that you give him no reason to doubt it."

"I will not."

"No. I did not think you would." Shen's eyes move for just a moment to the bench against the wall, and rest there, and move on again. "That is all I have. The Hall thanks the house of Lin for its patience."

* * *

In the corridor outside, the registrar's boy hands Father a sealed receipt and Wenshi a sealed receipt for the guard's rolls, and in the confusion of the exchange Jian slips through the open door of the records room and stands at the end of a shelf, with a sleeping sister in his arms and a very good reason to be there.

It is a long narrow room, high-ceilinged and smelling of dust and camphor, with shelves stacked to the beams. Ledgers lie in rows. Each family in the valley has its own: the tributary houses, the independent cultivators, the guards, the merchants. The Lin ledger is on the third shelf, the spine marked with a pine crest in faded gilt. The boy who handed out the receipts has left it on the desk by the window, open to a recent page.

Jian does not touch it. He does not need to. He has been reading upside down since he was three.

Lin Wenyuan. Patriarch. Entered this day.

Below that, a column of small entries in a clerk's hand. He reads them quickly, with the part of his mind that is cold and quick and does not feel anything. Most of them are routine. Tribute received. Seals verified. A guard captain's deposit of lance-points. Then near the bottom, one that makes him go very still.

Inquiry — Red Ridge steward Zhao Bei — re: Lin Jian, second son. First request, day after the midsummer incident: character, teacher, root. Second request, third month of this year: whether the boy has left the hill, in whose company. Reply to both: pseudo-root, no known teacher outside the house, one tutor, Old Hu, mortal artisan of no rank.

Third request, last month: whether the boy has been seen at Willow Ford.

Three inquiries. A steward from Red Ridge has been asking the Hall about a nine-year-old with five dim crystals, three times in ten months, and each time the answer has been nothing. And each time the Hall has written it down.

He feels the cold in his chest slide very gently into something clearer, and lower, and much more careful.

Not interested in a pseudo-root. Interested in a boy who counts.

Then Yue stirs on his shoulder, and he turns and carries her out into the corridor as though he had been looking for the privy.

* * *

On the way home, Feng does not speak until they have left the plain.

The road climbs back into the pines, and the evening comes down gold and slow through the branches. The guards have fallen back to a respectful distance. Father rides ahead on the mule, humming something tuneless under his breath. Mother walks at the cart's tail, her hat tipped low.

Feng walks beside the wheel, spear on his shoulder. After a mile he says, "He was going to hurt you."

"Who?"

"Qian." Feng's voice is low. "In the yard. He had that look. The one he had at the ring, before I cut his wrist." He glances sideways. "I did not hear you say anything. I thought you were going to be sick."

"I was holding a plum."

"You were holding a plum so hard it exploded." A short breath that is almost a laugh. "Radish. I am going to the Outer Court in a month. I am going to be gone for a long time. When I come back I will be a different person. I do not know what I will be. I am a little afraid of it." He shifts the spear. "I do not want to leave and find that something has happened to you while I was learning to be an inner disciple."

"Nothing will happen."

"Something is always going to happen. That is how this house works." Feng stares ahead into the trees. "I have been thinking. When I am gone, you will be the only one on that hill who understands what Hu does. Who helps him. Who sees what the rest of us cannot." He shrugs. "I have not asked you what it is. I will not. I want you to know that I have noticed there is something, and I think it is a good something. That is all."

Jian walks beside the wheel in the green dusk, the dried plum stain still sticky on his sleeve.

"You are going to be a very strong man, Elder Brother," he says.

"I know. I am the heir."

"You are also going to be careful."

"I am?" Feng looks at him with real surprise.

"Yes. For me." He keeps his eyes on the road. "I will make you a talisman for the Outer Court. A good one. Do not use it unless you really need to."

For a long time, Feng says nothing. Then, gruffly, he drops one hard, heavy hand on Jian's head and ruffles his hair, as he did when Jian was three.

"All right," he says. "I will be careful."

They climb on together into the dark pines. At the top of the ridge the road turns, and the valley opens below them in a long blue slope, with the wall of Green Pine Hill a pale thread against the hillside and the granary chimney already smoking, a small gray feather against the stars.

At the far end of the valley, on a spur two ridges west, a single light burns on the slope of Red Ridge.

Jian looks at it for a long time. He is not afraid of it, exactly. He is something quieter than afraid.

Three inquiries. One of them was last month.

Somebody is closing a circle. I would like to know how big it is before it closes.
